title: [Question] Which vLLM Ascend version is compatible with Speculators 0.8.0
body:
Hi, I would like to use Speculators 0.8.0 for speculative decoding and serve the trained draft model with vLLM Ascend. However, I cannot find a clear compatibility statement that specifies which vLLM Ascend version(s) work with Speculators 0.8.0.

The vLLM Ascend release compatibility matrix lists mappings for vLLM Ascend, upstream vLLM, Python, CANN, PyTorch/torch_npu, etc., but it does not appear to include Speculators. The Speculators documentation mentions integration with vLLM through vllm serve, but I could not find any vLLM Ascend-specific version constraints or known issues.

title: Training a draft on a Mamba-backbone verifier fails: KeyError: 'embed_tokens.weight'
body:
### What happened
Building a draft against `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16` fails at verifier-weight load with `KeyError: 'embed_tokens.weight'`. I reproduced it end-to-end with eagle3 and dflash on a recent `main` checkout. It is independent of `--draft-config`, since the load happens in the model base.

### Root cause
`SpeculatorModelBase._load_verifier_weights` (`src/speculators/model.py`) requests `embed_tokens.weight` and resolves it via `_resolve_key` / `_WEIGHT_ALIASES` (`src/speculators/utils/loading.py`). HF-format Mamba-backbone checkpoints name the input embedding `backbone.embeddings.weight`: NemotronH (verified on the published Nano, Super and Ultra checkpoints) and Mamba / Mamba2 / FalconMamba (per their transformers `modeling_*.py`). None of the current candidates (`embed_tokens.weight`, `tok_embeddings.weight`, `llm.embed.weight`) is a suffix of that key, so `_resolve_key` returns `None` and the subsequent lookup raises.

All algorithms on current `main` (eagle3, peagle, mtp, dflash, dflash2, dspark) load the verifier embedding through this method, so all are affected.

Llama-style hybrids (Bamba, Jamba, Zamba2) use `model.embed_tokens.weight` and are unaffected. Original `mamba_ssm`-format exports (`backbone.embedding.weight`, singular) are out of scope; this concerns HF/transformers-format checkpoints.

### Repro
    from speculators.utils.loading import _resolve_key
    _resolve_key("embed_tokens.weight", {"backbone.embeddings.weight": "x", "lm_head.weight": "x"})  # -> None

Code references: `main` @ `ad36840`. transformers 5.16.1.

### Context
The README lists Nemotron 3 Super/Ultra DFlash speculators, and their model cards document a `scripts/train.py --speculator-type dflash ...` recipe. Their verifiers also expose the embedding only as `backbone.embeddings.weight` (checked via the safetensors indices), and no released version of speculators resolves that key, so the recipe as written would hit this same error.

### Question
Is there an intended path for Mamba-backbone verifiers that I've missed (a flag, example or config override)? If not, I'd propose adding `backbone.embeddings.weight` to `_WEIGHT_ALIASES["embed_tokens.weight"]`, following #989, #719 and #1038. I have a PR ready (one alias plus resolver unit tests) and can open it if that approach works for you.

title: [RFC]: Agent-assisted RFC implementation via @claude in issue comments
body:
### Motivation.

The RFC-to-PR cycle involves manual effort that an agent could accelerate. vllm already uses Copilot SWE Agent; all four repos have Copilot code review. We'd like to add agent-assisted implementation to speculators, triggered by a human in issue comments — not autonomously.

### Proposed Change.

Add a GitHub Actions workflow so a maintainer can invoke an agent from an RFC issue comment (e.g. `@claude implement this` or `@copilot`). The agent reads the RFC, implements, runs `make quality` + `pytest`, and opens a **draft** PR linking the issue. A human reviews and checks the "I (a human) have reviewed the code" box before marking ready.

**Two options:**

| | Claude Code Action | Copilot SWE Agent |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | `@claude` in comments | Assign to Copilot / `@copilot` |
| Config | Custom system prompts, MCP tools | Minimal |
| Precedent | Not yet used in our repos | Already in vllm |
| Setup | Workflow file + API key | Toggle in repo settings |

**Scope:** Pilot in speculators, expand later if it works.

### Any Other Things.

1. Is Copilot SWE Agent the team-wide standard, or can repos choose their own tooling?
2. Any preference between the two options?
3. Comfortable with agent-generated draft PRs given the human-review checkbox?

title: DFlash raises AttributeError for verifiers without layer_types / sliding_window (Mistral, OLMo-2, Starcoder2)
body:
`DFlashSpeculatorModel.__init__` reads `tl_config.layer_types` and `tl_config.sliding_window` unconditionally. Both are optional in `transformers` — declared only when attention alternates, or when there is a window — so DFlash raises `AttributeError` in its constructor for verifiers with uniform global attention, before any draft layer is built.

[`dflash/core.py#L102-L107`](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/models/dflash/core.py#L102-L107)

### Reproduction

```python
from transformers import AutoConfig

for model_type in ("mistral", "olmo2", "starcoder2"):
    config = AutoConfig.for_model(model_type)
    print(model_type, hasattr(config, "layer_types"), hasattr(config, "sliding_window"))
```

```
AttributeError: 'MistralConfig' object has no attribute 'layer_types'
```

### Fix

```python
self.sliding_window = getattr(tl_config, "sliding_window", None)
self.sliding_window_indices = [
    i
    for i, layer_type in enumerate(getattr(tl_config, "layer_types", None) or [])
    if layer_type == "sliding_attention"
]
```

Identical behaviour for configs that declare them; `uses_sliding_window_attn` stays `False` for those that don't.

Branch ready with DCO sign-off; opening the issue first per CONTRIBUTING.

title: [Question] Why choose `guidellm` instead of `vllm bench` for speculator evaluation?
body:
Hi Authors,

I'm curious about the design choice of using `guidellm` for speculative decoding evaluation.

In my testing, `vllm bench` already supports key metrics like acceptance length, position-wise acceptance, TTFT/TPOT, and throughput. Switching to `vllm bench` alone would seem to reduce both code complexity and dependencies.

Are there specific technical reasons (e.g., metric consistency, guided generation support, or fairness in comparison) for preferring `guidellm` in this context?

Thanks for clarifying!

title: [RFC]: Add rasyosef/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-DSpark (5.53 accept length on math_reasoning) to the RedHatAI Speculator Models collection
body:
Would you be open to adding [Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-DSpark]( https://huggingface.co/rasyosef/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-DSpark) to the [RedHatAI Speculator Models collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/RedHatAI/speculator-models) on HuggingFace? 

It was trained using the `speculators` library on `100k samples` form the `open-perfectblend` dataset, and achieves a mean acceptance length of **3.27** tokens committed per verification step; **5.05** on `HumanEval`; **5.53** on `math_reasoning`.

Training code available on Github:  [rasyosef/train-dspark-draft-models](https://github.com/rasyosef/train-dspark-draft-models).


# Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-DSpark

A **DSpark draft model** for speculative decoding with [`unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct`](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) as the verifier, trained with [`speculators`](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators). The drafter proposes 8 tokens at a time and the verifier checks them in one forward pass, so output is identical to running the verifier alone — a lossless speedup. Mean acceptance length is **3.41** tokens committed per verification step, up to **5.53** on math_reasoning.

Training code: [rasyosef/train-dspark-draft-models](https://github.com/rasyosef/train-dspark-draft-models).

> Trained on 100,000 samples.

## Usage

vLLM loads the verifier automatically from the config — don't pass it separately.

```bash
vllm serve rasyosef/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-DSpark --port 8000 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8
```

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at `http://localhost:8000/v1`.

## Details

5 Qwen3 layers (hidden size 3072, intermediate size 8192, 24 attention heads over 8 KV heads, sliding-window attention with a 2048-token window), ~0.9B params, bfloat16. Block size 8, draft vocabulary reduced to 50,000, aux hidden-state layers 2/8/14/20/26, confidence head with Markov (rank 256).

Trained for 3 epochs at lr 3e-4 (AdamW, cosine schedule with 4% warmup) on 100,000 [Open PerfectBlend](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mlabonne/open-perfectblend) prompts regenerated by the verifier itself, split 96/4 into train and validation, with a `{"ce": 0.1, "tv": 0.9}` loss. Prompts prepared at 1024 tokens; training sequence length 8192, up to 1024 anchors per sample. Verifier hidden states were pulled on demand from a running vLLM server during training and deleted after use rather than staged to disk up front. speculators `0.8.0.dev207`, vLLM `0.28.0`, transformers `5.15.1`, torch `2.13.0`.

## Evaluation

`evaluate.py throughput` across the nine [`RedHatAI/speculator_benchmarks`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/RedHatAI/speculator_benchmarks) subsets. `acceptance_length` is mean tokens committed per verification step, including the bonus token — floor 1.0, ceiling 9.0 at block size 8.

| subset | acceptance_length | pos_0 | pos_1 | pos_2 | pos_3 | pos_4 | pos_5 | pos_6 | pos_7 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| math_reasoning | 5.529 | 89.6% | 78.4% | 67.9% | 58.8% | 50.5% | 43.3% | 36.0% | 28.2% |
| HumanEval | 5.058 | 85.6% | 72.6% | 61.6% | 52.3% | 43.7% | 36.3% | 29.9% | 23.8% |
| tool_call | 3.492 | 73.6% | 54.2% | 39.5% | 28.6% | 20.8% | 14.8% | 10.5% | 7.2% |
| question | 2.952 | 67.7% | 43.8% | 28.8% | 19.7% | 13.8% | 10.0% | 6.8% | 4.6% |
| rag | 2.917 | 67.6% | 45.8% | 30.8% | 20.4% | 12.6% | 7.6% | 4.4% | 2.4% |
| writing | 2.908 | 67.5% | 43.3% | 28.0% | 18.7% | 13.0% | 9.3% | 6.4% | 4.5% |
| translation | 2.653 | 67.0% | 42.7% | 25.2% | 14.2% | 7.9% | 4.4% | 2.6% | 1.3% |
| summarization | 2.597 | 65.6% | 40.5% | 23.9% | 13.9% | 8.0% | 4.3% | 2.2% | 1.2% |
| qa | 2.241 | 55.0% | 31.6% | 17.9% | 9.4% | 5.0% | 2.7% | 1.6% | 0.8% |

**Weighted across all subsets: 3.412** over 69,061 verification steps.

Acceptance is still highest where the verifier's next token is most predictable — math, code, structured tool calls. math_reasoning leads HumanEval by about half a token and holds a margin at every position in the block; math_reasoning's pos_5 (43.3%) is above summarization's pos_1 (40.5%), and both subsets still commit better than one token in four at pos_7. tool_call sits on its own at 3.49, between the two groups.

Five of the six prose-like subsets start in a tight band at pos_0 (65.6–67.7%) and separate only deeper into the block; qa is the exception, starting well below the rest at 55.0% and staying last throughout. question and writing decay gently and are still above 4% at pos_7. rag has the strongest pos_1 of the group (45.8%) but falls away after pos_3, and summarization, translation, and qa are all under 1.5% at pos_7 — so the tail of the block is worth something on open-ended generation but essentially nothing on summarization, translation, and qa.

## Limitations

Works only with `Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct` and is not usable as a standalone model. Acceptance falls off steeply past the first few positions on prose-like traffic (summarization, translation, qa), so a block size of 8 is mostly wasted there — the gains concentrate in math, code, and tool calls. Real-world speedup depends on your traffic mix, and because verification is lossless, the verifier's own behavior and biases carry through unchanged.

## License

Llama 3.2 Community License, inherited from the verifier. The `speculators` training code is Apache-2.0.

title: [Question]: DFlash2 multimodal acceptance gap with mixed text+MM training — text deploy ≥ train val, but ALLaVA deploy −10%
body:
### Summary

DFlash2 draft trained on MIXED text + multimodal data. Text deployment matches/exceeds training val, but
multimodal deployment is systematically lower — and ORACLE decomposition shows
the draft and selector are NOT degraded. Root cause appears to be path
divergence amplified by multimodal next-token uncertainty, not draft quality.

### Setup

- Verifier: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-w8a8 (MoE, W8A8, Ascend NPU, TP8+DP2)
- Draft: DFlash2 5-layer (conv_kernel_size=2, selector_top_k=16, block_size=8),
  trained on MIXED text + multimodal data (pure text + image prompts),
  `--loss-fn kl_div` + selector CE, teacher-forced
- Deployment: vLLM (speculators-based fork) 0.27.2rc1, greedy (temp=0), c=1
- Test sets: GSM8K (1319), MATH-500 (500), ALLaVA (100, 1 image each)

### Results (same checkpoint, c=1 greedy, accept_len includes +1 bonus token)

| Eval set | N | type | accept_rate | accept_len |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Train val (self_cond path) | - | - | - | **4.310** |
| GSM8K | 1319 | text deploy | **0.6298** | **5.408** |
| MATH-500 | 500 | text deploy | **0.6022** | **5.215** |
| ALLaVA | 100 | 1-img deploy | 0.4074 | **3.852** |

- Text deploy accept_len (5.41 / 5.22) > train val (4.31) — text path is healthy
- Multimodal ALLaVA deploy (3.85) < train val (4.31) — **−10%**
- accept_rate is token-level (accepted / draft_tokens), bonus-free in all rows

### ORACLE decomposition (ALLaVA, 67 requests)

Both draft and selector are NOT degraded:
- trunk_topK_hit (candidate contains target): pos0=1.0 → pos6=0.729
  (better than train val recall 0.847)
- selector_hit (picks correct): pos0=0.847 → pos6=0.494
  (≈ train teacher_forced_selector_acc 0.666)

So the acceptance gap is NOT caused by a broken draft/selector — it is
autoregressive path divergence: once the draft guesses wrong at an early
position, the block-internal context deviates from the training distribution,
and multimodal (image→text) mapping is much more ambiguous than text, so
errors compound faster.

### Questions

1. Training is MIXED text+MM, yet multimodal deployment still drops vs text.
   Is the remaining gap purely path divergence, or does mixed training itself
   under-fit the multimodal distribution?
2. Train val uses the `1-TV` upper bound (distribution overlap) while
   deployment requires argmax agreement. For multimodal flat distributions,
   is the val metric systematically optimistic?
3. Would switching unary loss from `kl_div` to `nla`/`tv` (argmax-aligned)
   or adding more multimodal data to the mix narrow this gap?

### Environment

- Ascend NPU, CANN 9.0.1, vLLM 0.27.2rc1.dev92, speculators 0.8.0.dev208
- Can provide config.json / train_command.txt / reproduction data

title: EAGLE-3 fails on any MoE verifier: Eagle3FirstLayerMixin adds a tuple to a tensor
body:
`Eagle3FirstLayerMixin.forward` assumes `self.mlp` returns a tensor. MoE blocks in `transformers` return `(hidden_states, router_scores)`, so the residual add one line later raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'Tensor' and 'tuple'`. EAGLE-3 is therefore unusable with any MoE verifier.

[`model_definitions.py#L106-L109`](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/models/eagle3/model_definitions.py#L106-L109)

```python
hidden_states = self.mlp(hidden_states)      # tuple for MoE
hidden_states = residual + hidden_states     # TypeError
```

### Reproduction

```python
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM

config = AutoConfig.for_model("gpt_oss", num_hidden_layers=1, hidden_size=64,
                              num_attention_heads=4, num_key_value_heads=2,
                              intermediate_size=128)
with torch.device("meta"):
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(config)
print(type(model.get_decoder().layers[0].mlp).__name__)  # GptOssMLP -> returns a tuple
```

### Fix

```python
mlp_output = self.mlp(hidden_states)
hidden_states = mlp_output[0] if isinstance(mlp_output, tuple) else mlp_output
```

Dense verifiers are unaffected. The rest of the rewrite already works for gpt-oss — the patched q/k/v feed `self.sinks` and `o_proj` unchanged and attention returns a correct tensor.

Branch ready with DCO sign-off; opening the issue first per CONTRIBUTING.

title: DFlash2 asserts an exact layer class, making the documented _make_decoder_layer override unusable
body:
`DFlashDraftModel._make_decoder_layer` is documented as the override point for DFlash-family variants, but `DFlash2SpeculatorModel.__init__` then asserts every layer is exactly `Qwen3DFlash2DecoderLayer`, so overriding it raises `AssertionError`.

[`dflash2/core.py#L51-L53`](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/models/dflash2/core.py#L51-L53)

```python
for layer_ in self.layers:
    assert isinstance(layer_, Qwen3DFlash2DecoderLayer)
    layer_.reset_convolutions()
```

The assertion is stronger than the next line needs — that only requires a layer able to reset its convolutions — and as an `assert` it is stripped under `python -O`.

### Fix

```python
if not hasattr(layer_, "reset_convolutions"):
    raise TypeError(
        f"{type(layer_).__name__} has no reset_convolutions(); a DFlash2 "
        "decoder layer must wrap its sublayers in resettable convolutions."
    )
layer_.reset_convolutions()
```

Same protection, and the documented override works.

### Context

A generic decoder layer with your unmodified `GroupedDynamicCausalConv` as its two sublayer wrappers reproduces `Qwen3DFlash2DecoderLayer` to 4.0e-06 on a 12.6 scale. (The convolutions have to be randomised first — `reset_parameters()` initialises them as identity, so an init-only comparison proves nothing.) This assertion is the only thing blocking it.

Branch ready with DCO sign-off; opening the issue first per CONTRIBUTING.

title: [Bug]: Training shutdown decorator leaves signal handlers installed after return or error
body:
### Bug

At `3419401a380db305ed6493ba4680ad8a3c3e0e45`, `with_graceful_shutdown()` installs SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers but restores them only when it catches `TrainingInterruptedError`. After a normal return or an unrelated exception, the installed handlers still belong to the completed training call.

This matters when invoking training from a longer-lived Python process: a later interrupt enters the stale training handler, rather than the handler that was active before training. Repeated/nested decorated calls can also capture and restore stale handlers.

### Minimal reproduction

From a checkout, this uses only Python's standard library and loads the actual production file. It avoids unrelated package initialization and restores the process's handlers before exiting.

```python
import runpy
import signal

module = runpy.run_path("src/speculators/train/graceful_shutdown.py")
before = {sig: signal.getsignal(sig) for sig in (signal.SIGINT, signal.SIGTERM)}

@module["with_graceful_shutdown"]()
def train(self):
    return "finished"

try:
    print(train(object()))
    print({sig.name: signal.getsignal(sig) == handler
           for sig, handler in before.items()})
finally:
    for sig, handler in before.items():
        signal.signal(sig, handler)
```

Observed on Windows / Python 3.13:

```text
finished
{'SIGINT': False, 'SIGTERM': False}
```

Expected: both values are `True`. Raising an ordinary `RuntimeError` inside the decorated call also leaves the handlers installed.

### Proposed scope and verification

A minimal fix is to add an outer `finally: handler.restore()` to the existing try/except, preserving the early restore before interrupt-checkpoint saving. A local two-line fix plus six regression cases covers return values, ordinary exceptions, `KeyboardInterrupt`, checkpoint success/failure, and nested calls.

Isolated tests loading the real stdlib-only module: **4 failed / 2 passed before**, **6 passed after**. A tiny CUDA linear-model workload also reproduces the leak and verifies restoration after the fix for FP32/BF16 and return/error paths; this is **not** a full Speculators Trainer or distributed-training test.

The standard pytest entry point is currently blocked on this Windows environment by the package's `fcntl` import. A follow-up PR still needs the contributor's human review/sign-off and supported-environment checks. This report was prepared with coding-agent assistance; no human-review checklist is being asserted here.

title: [RFC]: Pretrain DFlash-family drafts on raw text before distillation
body:
## 1. Motivation

A draft's data budget is bounded by target-model compute, not by available text. Distillation needs on-policy regeneration and hidden-state extraction before training starts — two passes over the target, one of them autoregressive.

Pretraining needs neither. The draft predicts the corpus's next tokens from its frozen copy of the verifier's input embedding. The verifier contributes weights and is never run.

A large pretraining run is therefore cheap per token, and should let the on-policy stage get away with less data and fewer epochs — better generalization, and hopefully less total compute for equivalent acceptance.

Even at equal total compute, the pretrained base is reusable. It learns from the embedding alone, so it commits to nothing about which aux hidden-state layers a finetune will read, or how many. One base can be widened to several selections and feed an entire layer sweep, and in principle adapted to DFlash, DFlash2 and DSpark, which share a backbone.

## 2. Results

Qwen3-8B, DFlash. Finetune data is on-policy regenerated with the target (UltraChat, Tulu3, Magpie, Nemotron, MetaMathQA, OrcaMath, evol-codealpaca, AutoIF, LMSYS-Arena). Within each table, runs differ only in `--from-pretrained` — same data, steps, schedule, seed.

**15M-token finetune**, 407 steps:

| pretrain | val loss | val EAL | test MAL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 1.437 | 0.643 | 1.697 |
| 100M | 1.370 | 0.732 | 1.805 |
| 3B | 1.292 | 0.837 | 1.950 |
| 20B | 1.255 | 0.909 | 2.063 † |

**111M-token finetune**, 4070 steps:

| pretrain | val loss | val EAL | test MAL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 1.021 | 1.548 | 2.702 |
| 20B | 0.969 | 1.745 | 2.957 |

Monotone on every column, and test MAL improves on all nine eval subsets in both tables. Running the 20B warm start for 3 epochs instead of 1 reaches val EAL 1.929 / MAL 3.239 — more compute, so not controlled, but the gain does not saturate.

The benefit narrows as finetune data grows: val EAL improves +41% at 15M tokens against +13% at 111M. Pretraining buys the most where on-policy data is scarce or expensive.

Not established: a single verifier and architecture.

† Evaluated at concurrency 32 / 100 requests rather than 128 / 200. The 3B checkpoint was measured under both and differs by 0.005.

‡ Val EAL and test MAL are different estimators at this commit; compare down a column, not across.

## 3. Design

`--training-mode pretrain`, a root-level mode rather than a new speculator type. The initial PR covers the DFlash family.

Two substitutions inside the shared `_backbone_forward`: features come from `embed_tokens(input_ids)` instead of the dataloader's aux hidden states, and targets are hard token ids instead of verifier logits. DSpark and DFlash2 inherit both.

No new loss. `ce_loss` already reduces soft targets to their argmax, so a hard label is the same objective with the argmax skipped. `losses/targets.py` names the distinction — a target is soft logits `[1,T,V]` or token ids `[1,T]` — and the remaining soft-target consumers have exact point-mass forms: TV collapses to `1 - p_t` for DSpark's confidence head, and DFlash2's covered candidate mass collapses to whether the candidates contain the target.

`training_mode` is a call-time argument threaded through `get_trainer_kwargs`, never written to config. A pretrained checkpoint is therefore an ordinary DFlash checkpoint that `--from-pretrained` loads directly. There is no conversion step.

The warm start is exact. Pretraining runs with a single auxiliary layer and trains the `fc` columns fed by verifier layer 0 — the embedding. `speculators expand-aux-layers` then widens the projection to the selection distillation will use, leaving the new slots at zero, so distillation resumes from exactly the projection pretraining learned, with the aux contributions growing from nothing rather than from random init.

The trainer is untouched. A token budget fixes the sequence count, so the corpus stream defines `__len__` and the LR schedule resolves from it like any other run.

About 520 lines of source. EAGLE3 is deferred rather than precluded: it shares no `_backbone_forward`, so the feature substitution needs its own implementation, but the hard-label half already sits in `losses/targets.py` and is architecture-agnostic.

## 4. Constraints

**Block semantics must match across stages.** `block_size`, `sample_from_anchor` and `sliding_window_non_causal` differ pairwise across the DFlash-family defaults — dflash 16/False/False, dspark 8/True/False, dflash2 8/False/True. `sample_from_anchor` shifts which token each block slot predicts, so a pretrained base only transfers across algorithms if these are aligned.

The auxiliary-layer selection is chosen at the widening step, not at pretraining. `--from-pretrained` takes the ids from the checkpoint, so a distillation run's own `--target-layer-ids` is ignored, and vLLM must be launched extracting the same layers.

Verifiers that scale their embedding before layer 0 — Gemma by `sqrt(hidden_size)`, Granite by `embedding_multiplier` — are handled automatically; the draft applies the same factor, read from the verifier config.

Pretraining still needs the verifier's weights on disk — the embedding and LM head are read from the checkpoint — but never runs it.

## 5. Open questions

**Shared base, or pretrain per architecture?** Sharing requires manually aligning block semantics across the two stages, since the DFlash-family defaults differ pairwise, and it leaves DSpark's Markov head (78M params) and DFlash2's selector (96M) cold-starting. The Markov head consumes only previous-token ids and hidden states — both available during pretraining — and is essentially a token co-occurrence table, which is exactly what a corpus teaches. One ablation would settle whether sharing is worth the cold heads.

**Scheduler: WSD (#1056), and possibly WSM.** Linear decay bakes a horizon into the schedule, which is awkward when the horizon is a token budget you may want to extend or cut short — warmup-stable-decay removes that coupling. Warmup-stable-merge would go further: averaging checkpoints across the stable phase yields a usable model at any point without running a decay at all, so a long pretraining run can spin off a finetune whenever one is wanted rather than only at a planned end. That matters here because pretraining runs are long and the natural workflow is to branch finetunes off them as they go.

**Where do returns diminish, and what is the right split?** The gain rises with pretrain tokens and falls with finetune tokens, so there should be an efficient allocation between the two for a given compute budget. We have not looked for it, and the answer likely depends on how expensive on-policy regeneration is for the target.

## 6. Related work and status

- **#1015 (staged layer-selection pathway)** — a pretrained base carries no dependence on which aux layers a finetune picks, only on how many, so one base can serve an entire layer sweep rather than one run per candidate.
- **#1056 (warmup-stable-decay scheduler)** — see §5; pretraining is where the fixed-horizon assumption in the current schedulers actually hurts.
- **#694 (on-policy training roadmap)** — making regeneration the documented default raises exactly the cost §1 describes, which strengthens the case for a stage that skips it.
- **#708 (step-based iteration)** — token-budget runs are naturally step-based. This implementation sidesteps the need by giving the corpus stream a known length, so the epoch and LR schedule resolve normally, but a real step-based mode would subsume that.

Implementation is working end to end for DFlash, DSpark and DFlash2 — unit tests, docs, and an example recipe covering all three steps — on [`reed-meyerson/speculators@dflash-pretraining`](https://github.com/reed-meyerson/speculators/compare/vllm-project:35081a4...reed-meyerson:dflash-pretraining) (9 commits, 30 files, based on `35081a4`). It will be split into a reviewable PR stack if the direction is accepted. EAGLE3 is deferred to a follow-up.

title: [RFC]: Training-run integrity: skip steps on non-finite loss, log gradient norm, always persist the final checkpoint
body:
Three independent integrity gaps in the current training loop can each silently corrupt or lose a long training run. All three were hit in extended distributed training jobs of draft models, and none of them is observable from the outside until it is too late:

**1. A bad batch silently poisons the run.** `Trainer.train_epoch` runs `loss.backward()` and the optimizer step unconditionally. When one batch carries a non-finite loss (NaN/Inf activations, a numerically unstable target, an overflow under autocast), backward propagates the NaN into every gradient, the optimizer writes NaN/Inf moments, and from that step on the whole run is diverged. There is no warning: the loss log shows a NaN value, and everything before it was fine. At that point the only remedy is to notice it hours later and restart from an older checkpoint, re-paying all the compute in between. The data-side counterpart of this problem was already fixed in #994 (skip NaN hidden states instead of crashing); this RFC covers the step-side, which #994 cannot prevent (a finite batch can still produce a non-finite loss under bf16 autocast).

**2. Gradient norm is invisible.** `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(..., 1.0)` computes the pre-clip total norm and throws it away. A run whose warmup overshoots (spike to 50+ then recovery) or that sits on the edge of divergence looks statistically identical to a healthy run in the logged metrics, because the norm — the single most diagnostic signal — never reaches the metric log.

**3. The final epoch can vanish.** The end-of-epoch save goes through `maybe_save_checkpoint`, which skips epochs where `(epoch + 1) % checkpoint_freq != 0`. A run with `num_epochs=7, checkpoint_freq=3` finishes all 7 epochs of compute and exits with no checkpoint of epoch 6 — the model that the run was actually training for. It still exists in optimizer-visible memory only at the moment the process exits.

These are the three canonical ways a multi-day speculative-decoder training run loses work that is not attributable to hardware or crashes: a poisoned step, an unseen divergence, and a checkpoint window that never overlaps the last epoch.

## Proposed Change.

**1. Step-skip on non-finite loss (Megatron `found_inf` pattern).**

- Before backward, check `torch.isfinite(loss)`.
- In distributed training, all-reduce a 0/1 flag with `ReduceOp.MAX` so *every* rank makes the same decision; per-rank decisions would deadlock the gradient sync.
- If the flag is set: skip `zero_grad`/`backward`/clip/`optimizer.step`/`scheduler.step` for this step, log a warning with the global step and the loss value, and continue with the next batch. `global_step` still advances, so `max_steps` semantics are unchanged.
- The check is one fused scalar kernel + one 8-byte all-reduce per step; the all-reduce is skipped entirely in single-process training.

**2. Log the pre-clip gradient norm, and enable the backstop.**

- `metrics["grad_norm"]` receives the value returned by `clip_grad_norm_`, so it flows through the existing per-step metric reduction/normalization pipeline.
- `error_if_nonfinite=True` is passed to the clip: the loss check in (1) covers non-finite *losses*; a finite loss whose *gradient* overflows must not silently write corrupted optimizer state either. Raising at the clip converts "run quietly diverges" into "run fails loudly at the step that caused it".

**3. Always persist the final checkpoint.**

- `maybe_save_checkpoint` gains a `force` flag and returns `bool` (whether it saved).
- `run_training` tracks whether the final epoch was persisted by the regular freq-gated save; if it was not, it forces one save for the final epoch after the loop, including `training_state.json` and the human-readable symlink, so the artifact is resumable like any other.
- Intentionally scoped out: `save_best` runs are left alone (their keep-only-best cleanup governs what stays on disk, and the final save there would fight that design), and the epoch-loop side of `max_steps` stopping (that was #898, which was closed for unrelated complexity).

The same three behaviors were implemented and validated in a downstream trainer; the attached patch is the minimal upstream-shaped version. A working implementation is on branch `pr-b3-train-stability` (single commit, CPU-only tests, ready to be opened as a PR once this RFC gets a green light).

## Any Other Things.

- **Relationship to existing work:**
  - **#1026 / #1027 (per-rank RNG resume)** is complementary and orthogonal: this RFC concerns *whether a step is applied and whether the run's end state is durable*; RNG restore concerns *whether a resumed run replays identically*. Both are needed for the "resume equals uninterrupted" property; neither depends on the other.
  - **#1104 (max_steps as scheduler horizon)** is part of the same family of trainer-fidelity fixes; this RFC deliberately does not touch the scheduler.
  - **#739 (crash-safe checkpoints, completeness marker)** covers *atomicity of the checkpoint directory itself*. This RFC does not propose an alternative; once #739 lands, the forced final save here composes with it (the forced save would also publish the completeness marker via `maybe_save_checkpoint`).
  - **#898 (stop the epoch loop at max_steps)** forced a save with a different mechanism and was withdrawn; the final-save problem here is the *natural end of training* case, which needs no cursor plumbing — `run_training` simply knows when it has finished the last epoch.
- **Cost:** one `isfinite` check plus one scalar all-reduce per step (single-process: no collective at all), a few hundred bytes of extra metric log per step, and at most one additional checkpoint write per run.
- **Tests** (all CPU-only, no GPU required): NaN batch is skipped with a warning and the run continues; the distributed MAX-reduce path skips on any rank's flag; `grad_norm` appears in the train metrics on normal steps and is absent on skipped steps; a finite loss with a non-finite gradient raises at the clip; the final checkpoint is forced when `checkpoint_freq` would skip the last epoch; no duplicate save when the gate already covered the final epoch; the forced save is resumable (writes `training_state.json`).

title: [Bug]: speculators train crashes on heterogeneous per-layer verifier configs (e.g. Gemma 4)
body:
### Current environment

- **Speculators:** 0.9.0.dev18 (main)
- **Transformers:** 5.16.1 (any ≥ ~5.15, i.e. once `HeterogeneousConfigMixin` landed)
- **PyTorch:** 2.13.0
- **CUDA:** 13.x
- **Model (verifier):** `google/gemma-4-31B-it` (any heterogeneous config — see below)

### 🐛 Description of the bug

`speculators train` fails at config-build time whenever the verifier is a **heterogeneous per-layer config** (transformers ≥5.15). In the default draft-construction branch, `src/speculators/train/cli.py` reads per-layer attributes off the **global** verifier config. Since transformers ~5.15 puts `HeterogeneousConfigMixin` in the MRO of `PreTrainedConfig`, reading a per-layer attribute (`head_dim`, `num_key_value_heads`) off the global config of a model shipping a `per_layer_config` raises `AmbiguousGlobalPerLayerAttributeError` — which **subclasses `RuntimeError`, not `AttributeError`**, so `getattr(config, "head_dim", None)` does **not** swallow it.

Failing block in `train/cli.py`:

```
head_dim = getattr(verifier_config, "head_dim", None)          # :158  -> RAISES (first crash)
num_attention_heads = verifier_config.num_attention_heads      # :159  (global here, OK for gemma-4)
num_key_value_heads = verifier_config.num_key_value_heads      # :160  -> ALSO RAISES
```

The `getattr(..., None)` default never applies (the access itself raises), and handling only `:158` just moves the crash to `:160`.

**Minimal repro** (config only; no GPU/weights):

```
from transformers import AutoConfig
tc = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("google/gemma-4-31B-it").text_config
print(tc.is_heterogeneous)              # True
print(sorted(tc.per_layer_attributes))  # ['head_dim', 'num_key_value_heads']
getattr(tc, "head_dim", None)           # raises (not swallowed by the default)
```

```
transformers.integrations.heterogeneity.configuration_utils.AmbiguousGlobalPerLayerAttributeError:
'head_dim' is a per-layer attribute and may vary across layers. Access it via the individual layer
configs instead (e.g. config.per_layer_config[i].head_dim).
```

E2E: `speculators train --speculator-type dflash --verifier-name-or-path google/gemma-4-31B-it …` fails at `train/cli.py:158`.

### Scope / who this affects

Heterogeneity is data-driven at the base-config level, so this hits **any** current or future model shipping a `per_layer_config` — in transformers today: `gemma4`, `gemma4_unified`, `diffusion_gemma`, `step3p7`. I audited the other `head_dim` reads in speculators and they are **safe**: `models/dflash/model_definitions.py` and `models/eagle3/model_definitions.py` read the drafter's own homogeneous config, and `convert/eagle/eagle3_converter.py` reads a plain dict. **`train/cli.py` is the only vulnerable site.**

### Proposed fix

These reads only seed the draft's *own* default attention: they're hit solely in the default branch (overridden by `--draft-config` / `--from-pretrained`), where the draft's `transformer_layer_config` is built from the shaping flags. The real constraint is `hidden_size` — the residual-stream width the draft ingests, which is homogeneous and reads fine; `head_dim` / `num_key_value_heads` describe a layer's internal projections, not the width of its output, so they're free draft hyperparameters, not target facts to match. There's thus no "correct" global *or* per-layer value to recover — just a sensible default to pick.

When `verifier_config.is_heterogeneous`, resolve the affected attributes from a single concrete `verifier_config.per_layer_config[i]`, driven off `verifier_config.per_layer_attributes` (not a hardcoded name list) so it covers any per-layer attribute uniformly. Homogeneous configs keep the global read. This mirrors `convert/dflash/converter.py`'s concrete-per-layer read and retires the downstream `allow_global_per_layer_attribute_access` monkeypatch.

Default to the **modal** layer — on gemma-4-31B that's `head_dim=256` / `num_key_value_heads=16` (≈50/60 layers), the bulk geometry, giving a leaner/faster draft (draft latency is on the spec-decoding critical path). The minority full-attention shape (`512` / `4`) would only make the draft heavier with no acceptance-rate upside. Read from a single real layer so the trio stays internally consistent, and assert `num_attention_heads % num_key_value_heads == 0` (`num_attention_heads` stays a global read at `:159`) so a future model that also varies query-head count can't silently produce a malformed draft attention block.

Happy to open a small, focused, DCO-signed PR from a fork with a unit test using a fake heterogeneous config (touches `train/cli.py` + a test), per CONTRIBUTING.

title: [RFC]: Add Qwen3-ASR audio-conditioned speculator training support
body:
### Motivation.

Speculators supports multimodal dataset preprocessing and Qwen3-VL workflows, but it does not currently provide a documented and tested end-to-end training path for audio-language models such as Qwen3-ASR.

Qwen3-ASR contains a Qwen3 language model behind an audio encoder. Training a post-hoc draft model requires preserving the original audio request while the frozen verifier performs audio preprocessing, audio-tower inference, and language-model inference. The resulting expanded token IDs, loss mask, and audio-conditioned decoder hidden states can then use the standard Speculators training contract.

I have a working out-of-tree prototype validated with:

- Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf
- Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf
- EAGLE-3, DFlash, and P-EAGLE
- offline cached hidden states and online hidden-state generation
- multi-GPU DDP training
- vLLM speculative serving and ASR evaluation

 After training on LibriSpeech 960h, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B speculators increased single-H100 throughput at concurrency 8 by 51.9% for EAGLE-3, 93.2% for DFlash, and 59.0% for P-EAGLE over dense decoding.

### Proposed Change.

I propose adding Qwen3-ASR as the audio counterpart to the existing Qwen3-VL training integration. It should reuse the shared multimodal pipeline rather than introduce a separate ASR trainer.

The implementation would:

1. Support audio paths and URLs in the existing multimodal conversation format, with the transcription stored in the assistant turn.

2. Preserve the original audio messages throughout data preparation and hidden-state generation. vLLM remains responsible for chat-template rendering, audio decoding, feature extraction, placeholder expansion, audio-tower execution, and verifier inference.

3. Use vLLM as the authoritative source of expanded token IDs and strictly validate alignment between token IDs, loss masks, auxiliary hidden states, and final hidden states before training.

4. Reuse the existing generic `text_config` and nested-weight resolution for the Qwen3 decoder. Core Speculators code should remain capability-based and modality-generic, without scattered `model_type == "qwen3_asr"` branches.

5. Keep the Qwen3-ASR verifier and audio tower frozen. EAGLE-3, DFlash, P-EAGLE, and DSpark continue consuming the standard Speculators tensor contract through the existing online, offline, hybrid, and distributed training workflows.

6. Add generic audio preprocessing and alignment tests, a Qwen3-ASR online/offline end-to-end smoke test, and a small documented training example analogous to the current Qwen3-VL coverage.

### Any Other Things.

I have a working prototype and would be happy to implement this contribution. If this scope and architecture look appropriate, please assign the issue to me.

title: [Roadmap] On Policy Training
body:
## Motivation

The driver is exposure bias: off-policy multi-turn data conditions each turn on the dataset's responses rather than the target's, so every turn past the first is misaligned. Regenerating turn-by-turn against the on-policy prefix fixes this — and yields longer, more realistic context as a bonus.


## Topic

Ensure no cross-instance attention leakage

title: [Bug]: Eagle3 conversion writes randomly initialized weights when a checkpoint key does not match, instead of failing
body:
### Your current environment

- Speculators: `main` at `35081a4`
- PyTorch 2.11.0, Transformers 5.9.0, Python 3.13, Linux, CPU only
- No model download needed for the reproduction below

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`Eagle3Converter._save_converted_checkpoint` logs missing and unexpected keys as warnings and then saves anyway:

```python
missing_keys, unexpected_keys = model.load_state_dict(remapped_weights, strict=False)

if missing_keys:
    logger.warning(f"Missing keys in checkpoint: {missing_keys}")

if unexpected_keys:
    logger.warning(f"Unexpected keys in checkpoint: {unexpected_keys}")
```

A weight that the model expects but the checkpoint does not supply stays at its random initialization, and that tensor is what gets written to disk. The conversion still ends with `logger.success("Saved to: ...")`.

This is the failure that #358 and #360 fixed after the fact: "Conversion logic was failing, causing acceptance rate to be 0 for all tokens positions. Added renaming logic to convert midlayer to layer.0. This logic was falsely removed from our conversion code." A lost remap produced a checkpoint that converted cleanly, loaded cleanly, and only showed up as zero acceptance during evaluation.

The two newer converters treat the same condition as a hard error. `MTPConverter._save`:

```python
if unexpected:
    raise ValueError("Unexpected keys in extracted weights -- ...")
if missing:
    critical_missing = [k for k in missing if k.startswith("mtp_layers.")]
    if critical_missing:
        raise ValueError("Critical MTP layer weights missing after extraction. ...")
```

`DFlashConverter._save` does the same with a `_VERIFIER_FILLED_KEYS` allowlist. Only the Eagle3 path, which is the one most people run, still warns.

#### Reproduction

Rename a single weight key, which is the shape of the #360 regression, and convert twice:

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import patch

import torch
from safetensors.torch import load_file

from speculators.convert.eagle.eagle3_converter import Eagle3Converter
from speculators.convert.eagle.eagle3_legacy_model import Eagle3Speculator

H, I, V = 64, 128, 256
verifier_cfg = {"architectures": ["LlamaForCausalLM"], "max_position_embeddings": 512,
                "rope_theta": 500000.0, "vocab_size": V}
eagle_config = dict(target_vocab_size=V, hidden_size=H, intermediate_size=I,
                    num_attention_heads=4, num_key_value_heads=2, hidden_act="silu",
                    max_position_embeddings=128, initializer_range=0.02, rms_norm_eps=1e-6,
                    attention_bias=False, rope_theta=10000.0, mlp_bias=False, draft_vocab_size=V)

conv = Eagle3Converter()
with patch("speculators.convert.eagle.eagle3_converter.PretrainedConfig.get_config_dict",
           return_value=(verifier_cfg, {})):
    config = conv._build_eagle3_speculator_config(
        dict(eagle_config), "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", False, False, False, False, None)

    # a correct source checkpoint, built from the model itself
    ref = Eagle3Speculator(config=config, verifier=None, verifier_attachment_mode="detached",
                           reduce_vocab_size=True, has_drafter_embedding=True)
    src = {("midlayer." + k[len("layers.0."):] if k.startswith("layers.0.") else k): v.clone()
           for k, v in ref.state_dict().items()}
    intended = src["midlayer.mlp.up_proj.weight"].clone()

    # one weight key under a name the converter does not know
    src["midlayer.mlp.up_projection.weight"] = src.pop("midlayer.mlp.up_proj.weight")

    saved = []
    for _ in range(2):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
            out = conv._save_converted_checkpoint(config, dict(src), Path(td), True, True)
            saved.append(load_file(str(Path(out) / "model.safetensors"))["layers.0.mlp.up_proj.weight"].float())

print("run 1 == run 2                       :", torch.equal(saved[0], saved[1]))
print("run 1 == the weight in the checkpoint:", torch.equal(saved[0], intended.float()))
```

Current result:

```text
run 1 == run 2                       : False
run 1 == the weight in the checkpoint: False
```

Two conversions of the same input write different `up_proj` weights, because the tensor comes from the model's random initialization rather than from the checkpoint. Both runs log the two warnings and report success.

### Expected behavior

The conversion fails instead of writing a checkpoint whose weights did not come from the input.

I checked that this cannot break a valid conversion. Sweeping every valid combination of the flags that change which parameters the model owns (`norm_before_residual`, `norm_before_fc`, `fc_norm`, `norm_output`, `reduce_vocab_size`, `has_drafter_embedding`, skipping the `norm_before_fc` plus `fc_norm` pair the config rejects) gives 48 correct conversions, and every one of them reports no missing and no unexpected keys.

I would raise on missing keys and keep unexpected keys a warning, since a real checkpoint carrying a harmless extra tensor is plausible while a missing weight always means the saved model is partly random. Happy to raise on both if you prefer the stricter MTP behavior. I have the change and a regression test ready and can open a PR once you tell me which of the two you want.

Duplicate search before filing: `midlayer`, `missing keys`, `unexpected keys`, `converter validation`, `warns instead of raising`, `acceptance rate 0`, plus the open PRs touching `convert/eagle`. #636 is the only open PR there and it changes a config default.

AI assistance: I used Claude Code while investigating and to help draft this report. I ran the reproduction and the flag sweep myself.

title: [Bug]: Hardcoded Qwen3RMSNorm causes weight mismatch for non-Qwen3 models (e.g., Qwen3.5)
body:
### Your current environment

Please provide the following information about your environment if applicable:



### 🐛 Describe the bug

Description In `src/speculators/models/dflash/core.py at line 126`, the normalization layer is currently hardcoded to use `Qwen3RMSNorm`:
https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/models/dflash/core.py#L126
```
 self.norm = Qwen3RMSNorm(
            config.transformer_layer_config.hidden_size,
            eps=config.transformer_layer_config.rms_norm_eps,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
        )
```
If the target model is not Qwen3 (for instance, Qwen3.5), this hardcoded implementation leads to incorrect numerical results when loading the model weights.

Root Cause The RMSNorm implementations between Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 have fundamental structural differences in how the weight parameter is applied and initialized.

Here is the Qwen3RMSNorm implementation:
```
class Qwen3RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, eps: float = 1e-6) -> None:
        """
        Qwen3RMSNorm is equivalent to T5LayerNorm
        """
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(hidden_size))
        self.variance_epsilon = eps

    def forward(self, hidden_states: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        input_dtype = hidden_states.dtype
        hidden_states = hidden_states.to(torch.float32)
        variance = hidden_states.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True)
        hidden_states = hidden_states * torch.rsqrt(variance + self.variance_epsilon)
        return self.weight * hidden_states.to(input_dtype)

    def extra_repr(self):
        return f"{tuple(self.weight.shape)}, eps={self.variance_epsilon}"
```
And here is the Qwen3_5RMSNorm implementation:
```
class Qwen3_5RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim: int, eps: float = 1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(dim))

    def _norm(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)

    def forward(self, x):
        output = self._norm(x.float())
        # Llama does x.to(float16) * w whilst Qwen3_5 is (x * w).to(float16)
        # See https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/29402
        output = output * (1.0 + self.weight.float())
        return output.type_as(x)

    def extra_repr(self):
        return f"{tuple(self.weight.shape)}, eps={self.eps}"
```
Key Differences:

**1.Weight Initialization**: Qwen3RMSNorm initializes self.weight to ones, whereas Qwen3_5RMSNorm initializes to zeros.
**2.Forward Pass Calculation**:
Qwen3 calculates: self.weight * hidden_states
Qwen3.5 calculates: output * (1.0 + self.weight)
Because of these differences, if a Qwen3.5 checkpoint is force-loaded into a Qwen3RMSNorm module, the norm.weight values will mismatch mathematically. For example, a weight value of 0.5 in Qwen3.5 is meant to scale the output by 1.5 (1.0 + 0.5), but if loaded into Qwen3's module, it will scale the output by 0.5. This completely breaks the model's inference accuracy.

Suggested Fix The normalization layer should not be hardcoded to Qwen3RMSNorm. It should dynamically select the correct RMSNorm class based on the target model's architecture/configuration, or utilize a generic normalization wrapper that adapts to the specific weight format of the target model.

title: [Performance] DFLASH windowed-attention backward — flash-attn-style Triton operator
body:
### Proposal
This follows the "General Training Performance Improvements" initiative in the
Q3 Roadmap (#781, status: *Not Yet Started*) — this operator is a benchmarked
bottleneck fix for it.

A self-contained Triton operator for windowed-attention backward (flash-attention
style: two-pass online softmax + `atomic_add` for dK/dV). It respects the
anchor-block window and never materializes dense S/P. The integration diff is
available on request and will follow as a separate PR once the operator lands.

### Problem
The DFLASH draft attends each query only to an anchored block-windowed set of KV
blocks, but its backward currently goes through dense `flex_attention`,
materializing the full `[q_len, kv_len]` attention matrix. At production sizes the
dense backward needs ~69GB (OOM on 8×A800) and ignores the window structure.

### Benchmark (independent re-verification, 8×A800 SM80, torch 2.13.0+cu130)
| metric | dense flex backward | this operator |
|---|---|---|
| time | 419.2 ms | 184.7 ms (**2.3×**) |
| peak memory | ~69GB (OOM at prod size) | 5.6 GB (no dense materialization) |
| correctness | — | corr dq/dk/dv = 1.0000 (single- & cross-doc) |

(Additional BLOCK tuning: 997.8 → 137.4 ms, 7.26×.)
(Measured at a medium size that fits the dense baseline; at production size the
dense backward OOMs — that is the motivation.)

### Scope
- new file `windowed_attn_bwd.py` (~341 lines, imports only torch + triton)
- `DFlexAttnBwd` autograd wrapper; `non_causal` default aligned to production `False`
- integration intentionally NOT in this PR (follow-up): DFLASH decoder wiring,
  GQA-aware / amortized / 3-kernel-split variants, symmetric fused forward kernel

### Validation
- fwd+grad parity vs eager `flex_attention` (causal + non-causal, non-power-of-2 tail)
- A800 SM80

Is this the right direction for the DFLASH backward? Happy to split further or adjust scope.

title: [Bug]: Per-engine counter decreases can be hidden by aggregate acceptance deltas
body:
### Your current environment

- Windows, Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.1.3, SciPy 1.15.3 (the relevant utility imports NumPy; SciPy is optional).
- Synthetic CPU-only parser/extractor reproduction; no vLLM service, CUDA, PyTorch, Transformers, model, or training/evaluation workload is exercised.
- Local checkout commit `2cfe086`; `scripts/evaluate/perf_utils.py` Git blob `cc2001a795e2c1ba65ad76e44daedd3e06878ac2` matches current upstream when checked. `evaluate.py` blob also matches upstream: `f1214022fafd587557e24de35338bfedc355125b`.

### Describe the bug

Hi! Following up on the multi-engine aggregation work in #1096, I found a counter-continuity edge case. A decrease in one engine's counters can be hidden by growth in another engine, producing plausible positive aggregate acceptance metrics. Before changing evaluation behavior, could we agree on the intended handling?

Run the following Python snippet from the root of a Speculators checkout containing the utility above (NumPy required). It uses the real parser/extractor and synthetic engine-labelled snapshots; it does not launch a benchmark.

```python
import runpy

api = runpy.run_path("scripts/evaluate/perf_utils.py")

def snapshot(engines):
    lines = []
    for engine, (drafts, tokens, accepted) in engines.items():
        for name, value in (
            ("num_drafts", drafts),
            ("num_draft_tokens", tokens),
            ("num_accepted_tokens", accepted),
        ):
            lines.append(
                f'vllm:spec_decode_{name}_total{{engine="{engine}"}} {value}'
            )
        lines.append(
            'vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_per_pos_total'
            f'{{engine="{engine}",position="0"}} {accepted}'
        )
    return api["parse_prometheus_metrics"]("\n".join(lines))

baseline = snapshot({"a": (100, 200, 80), "b": (100, 200, 80)})
results = []
for name, engines in (
    ("masked decrease", {"a": (20, 40, 10), "b": (220, 440, 170)}),
    ("monotonic control", {"a": (120, 240, 90), "b": (120, 240, 90)}),
):
    result = api["extract_spec_decode_metrics"](snapshot(engines), baseline)
    print(name, result)
    assert result["num_drafts"] == 40
    assert result["acceptance_length"] == 1.5
    assert result["acceptance_at_pos_0"] == 0.5
    results.append(result)
assert results[0] == results[1]
```

Both cases return the same deltas: 40 drafts, 80 draft tokens, 20 accepted tokens, acceptance length 1.5, and position-0 acceptance 0.5. The positive draft count passes `_run_subset`'s report/CSV guard. Once series labels have been discarded during parsing/aggregation, a later aggregate-only check cannot distinguish these histories.

For comparison, when the aggregate draft delta is negative, `_run_subset` skips acceptance output with `No speculative decoding metrics found`. It does not print the extractor's zero acceptance result. This report is specifically about a decrease masked by positive aggregate growth.

### Expected behavior / scope question

Would you welcome retaining series identity until continuity validation and explicitly marking an interval invalid when a matching counter decreases? We should also agree on handling newly appearing/disappearing series, and whether an invalid interval should fail evaluation or omit acceptance metrics with a specific diagnostic while retaining other results.

I would avoid clamping negative deltas or reconstructing the full interval from post-reset values. Two endpoint scrapes cannot detect every reset, including one where the counter surpasses its baseline before the final scrape. This synthetic example is not evidence of an actual serving-process restart.

I checked #1082's smoothing changes and #1064's new MRCR runner. Neither adds continuity handling; the proposed MRCR path also uses this extractor, so any shared API change should account for that caller.

Happy to work on an agreed scope if this fits the roadmap. This investigation and report were prepared with AI assistance; no implementation, assignment, or completion is claimed.

title: [Bug]: acceptance_at_pos_i is under-counted when the target server runs with --data-parallel-size >= 2
body:
### Your current environment speculators: 0.9.0.dev6 vLLM: 0.28.0 Model: rasyosef/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-speculator.dspark GPUs: 2 Command: python evaluate.py throughput --target http://localhost:8000/v1 ### 🐛 Describe the bug

Bug: acceptance_at_pos_i is under-counted when the target server runs with --data-parallel-size >= 2

Summary

When evaluating against a vLLM server started with --data-parallel-size 2, the aggregate columns in the emitted acceptance.csv (num_drafts, num_draft_tokens, num_accepted_tokens, acceptance_length) look correct, but the per-position columns (acceptance_at_pos_0 ... acceptance_at_pos_3) are roughly a factor of dp_size too small.

The tell is that the two sets of numbers no longer agree with each other. For a run with k draft tokens per step, the following identity must hold:

acceptance_length == 1 + sum(acceptance_at_pos_i for i in range(k))

In the results below it is violated on every single subset, by a factor that hovers around 2 (the DP size used for the run).

Environment

  • speculators: 0.9.0.dev6
  • vLLM: 0.28.0
  • Model: rasyosef/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-speculator.dspark
  • GPUs: 2
  • Command: python evaluate.py throughput --target http://localhost:8000/v1

Reproduction

Serve the speculator with DP >= 2:

import subprocess, os

env = os.environ.copy()
env["PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF"] = "expandable_segments:True"

log_file = open("/content/vllm_serve.log", "w")
process = subprocess.Popen(
    [
        "vllm", "serve", "rasyosef/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-speculator.dspark",
        "--port", "8000",
        "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.90",
        "--data-parallel-size", "2",
    ],
    stdout=log_file,
    stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
    env=env,
    start_new_session=True,
)
print(f"Started vLLM server with PID {process.pid}")

import time, requests

for i in range(120):
    try:
        r = requests.get("http://127.0.0.1:8000/health")
        if r.status_code == 200:
            print("Server is ready!")
            break
    except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
        pass
    print(f"Waiting... ({i+1})")
    time.sleep(5)

Then run the evaluation:

python evaluate.py throughput --target http://localhost:8000/v1

Observed output (acceptance.csv)

Contents of acceptance.csv, rounded for readability:

subset | num_drafts | num_draft_tokens | num_accepted_tokens | acceptance_length | pos_0 | pos_1 | pos_2 | pos_3 -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- HumanEval | 22,861 | 91,444 | 38,819 | 2.6980 | 0.3584 | 0.2492 | 0.1639 | 0.1028 math_reasoning | 5,163 | 20,652 | 7,149 | 2.3847 | 0.3145 | 0.1935 | 0.1048 | 0.0548 qa | 7,839 | 31,356 | 6,051 | 1.7719 | 0.2101 | 0.0903 | 0.0425 | 0.0176 question | 15,292 | 61,168 | 15,642 | 2.0229 | 0.2834 | 0.1446 | 0.0770 | 0.0411 rag | 4,502 | 18,008 | 3,447 | 1.7657 | 0.2088 | 0.0931 | 0.0369 | 0.0155 summarization | 12,901 | 51,604 | 7,094 | 1.5499 | 0.2002 | 0.0663 | 0.0167 | 0.0040 tool_call | 39,412 | 157,648 | 49,494 | 2.2558 | 0.3508 | 0.2016 | 0.1028 | 0.0533 translation | 2,199 | 8,796 | 1,160 | 1.5275 | 0.1842 | 0.0582 | 0.0155 | 0.0009 writing | 16,936 | 67,744 | 18,711 | 2.1048 | 0.3015 | 0.1744 | 0.0797 | 0.0384

The two columns should be equal. Instead the ratio sits near dp_size = 2 on every subset. It is not exactly 2 because the two DP ranks serve different requests and therefore have genuinely different acceptance behaviour per subset — which is itself consistent with the positional numerator coming from a single rank while the denominator covers both.

Running the identical evaluation against a server with --data-parallel-size 1 makes the two columns agree. <!-- please confirm on your setup -->

Suspected cause

When --data-parallel-size > 1, vLLM exposes its speculative-decoding metrics as one series per engine/DP rank rather than a single series, i.e. spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_per_pos is emitted once per (position, engine) pair.

The scaling behaviour above is what you would get if the aggregate counters are summed over all series while the per-position counters are not — for example, if the per-position samples are collected into a dict keyed only on position, so each engine's sample overwrites the previous one and only the last rank scraped survives. The per-position numerator then reflects one rank while num_drafts in the denominator reflects all of them, giving the ~1/dp_size deflation.

Expected behaviour

Per-position acceptance counters should be summed across all DP ranks/engines before the rate is computed, so that acceptance_length == 1 + sum(acceptance_at_pos_i) holds regardless of --data-parallel-size.

Suggested fix

Where the metrics are parsed, aggregate over every matching sample rather than keyed assignment — something along the lines of:

# before: last engine wins
per_pos[pos] = sample.value

# after: accumulate across engines / DP ranks
per_pos[pos] = per_pos.get(pos, 0.0) + sample.value

Two things worth adding alongside the fix:

  1. An assertion or warning when abs(acceptance_length - 1 - sum(acceptance_at_pos)) > tol, which would have surfaced this immediately.
  2. A regression test that scrapes a metrics payload containing duplicated per-position series under different engine labels and asserts they are summed.

Workaround

Serve with --data-parallel-size 1 for evaluation runs (use tensor parallelism instead if the model needs to be sharded). The aggregate acceptance_length from the DP >= 2 runs appears trustworthy; only the positional breakdown should be discarded.

title: Add unit tests, type annotations, and docstrings for speculators.train utilities (noise_transforms.py and vocab_mapping.py)
body:
### Motivation.

The training subsystem relies on two lightweight utility modules for data preparation and augmentation: [`src/speculators/train/noise_transforms.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/train/noise_transforms.py) and [`src/speculators/train/vocab_mapping.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/train/vocab_mapping.py). Both have incomplete test coverage and typing/docstring discrepancies:

1. **`noise_transforms.py`**:
   - Defines `TransformTensors`, `AddGaussianNoise`, and `AddUniformNoise` used for hidden state augmentation.
   - It is a 26-line file that currently lacks docstrings, full type annotations on `__init__` and `__call__`, and does not define `__all__`.
   - There are **zero unit tests** in the entire test suite covering this module.

2. **`vocab_mapping.py`**:
   - `save_token_frequency_distribution()` docstring states:
     ```
     Returns:
         Path to the saved frequency distribution file
     ```
     However, the function returns `None` (either early returning `return` or terminating without returning `path`).
   - `__all__` only lists 2 of the 4 functions defined in the module, omitting `combine_token_frequency_distributions` and `get_target_vocab_size`.
   - In `combine_token_frequency_distributions`, `combined_token_freq` is typed as `Counter[str] = Counter()`, even though token IDs are integers (`Counter[int]`).
   - While `test_vocab_mapping_cli.py` tests CLI argument parsing and caching, there are no direct unit tests validating `build_vocab_mappings_from_distribution()` (verifying offset tensor math, frequency sorting, and fallback padding) or `combine_token_frequency_distributions()`.

Consolidating these into one issue provides a well-rounded contribution to the training pipeline utilities that runs entirely on CPU.

### Proposed Change.

#### Part 1: `src/speculators/train/noise_transforms.py`
